utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. All the accused are present. Defence teams are all here. Witness is present, too. Mr. McCloskey is present for the Prosecution, and for the Defence the forensic expert, Mr. Dunjic is also present. Professor, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, I would like to explain why we are starting a quarter of an hour late. That's because we are informed that this morning the -- some members of the Defence teams, I don't know exactly who, made it known that they intended to make use of some documents, which so happened the witness did not -- was not carrying with him when he had arrived here. So we allowed him time to go back to his hotel and bring them over, which I understand you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I thank you, Professor. So Mr. McCloskey, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. President, I had finished up under the 92 bis system, and so ready for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood, okay. You don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So who is going first? Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I can indicate that was my request for Professor Wright to provide his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not relevant. Whoever's request it was, it's a legitimate request which had to be met.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Professor Wright, can I just ask when was the first time you were engaged by the Tribunal to engage in the -- in the digging at the sites?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: At which site?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Which was the first site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the first site, it was at Brcko, and we started work, if my memory serves me correctly, in April 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's not a grave that relates to this case.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: In relation to this particular case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to this particular case, the first site that we went to was what I called the Red Dam, and that was in April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, prior to you attending at the site and engaging in the dig, what information or briefing had you received, if at all, from any investigator attached to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was told that this was believed to be a place of execution, and that bodies had been buried in a grave in the front of the dam, in the rocky platform in front of the dam, and that this grave was undisturbed at the time when other primary graves were exhumed and the bodies taken away. We started excavations there and very soon concluded that it had been disturbed, and that it was a primary grave that had been robbed, there were body parts left, but that was all. And I told the -- the investigators that I disagreed with the proposal that this was an undisturbed primary grave, and they then went and got more aerial images from the people who provided them with aerial images and found that one had been missed, not I think by the investigators, but by the suppliers of the images that showed that it had in October been -- been robbed. So that was the first job I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, the source of that original information, was that from Mr. Ruez, the chief investigator?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much from Mr. Ruez, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Was he actually present on this first dig at Red Dam?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly for part of the time, but I can't remember how often. He wasn't there the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Can I just take you back a little bit to what you said in an answer is that to clarify that initially it was conveyed to you that this was an undisturbed primary grave, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And that was based upon the information that had been gleaned in the -- through the aerial imagery, as you understand it, is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And then as a consequence of your assessment at the actual site, you deemed that to be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a consequence of our actual excavation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The excavation, yes. Is it possible at all to make that assessment without having engaged in the exhumation? Is it ever possible to make that -- I'll make my question a little more clear. Is it ever possible to make that assessment about a grave being a secondary grave without engaging in a full exhumation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, can I point out this was a primary grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it has been robbed or not, it may be possible to do that by examining the surface after scraping, whether it's been robbed or not, But it wasn't ever thought to be a secondary grave. It's a primary grave. I would say I would feel uncomfortable of making that assessment without examining the soil itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So to clarify, what the initial assessment was an undisturbed primary grave; and as a result of your exhumation, it went to being a disturbed primary grave. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, given what you were -- well, can I ask you this: That information that Mr. Ruez gave you as to the dam being a site of alleged or mass grave in relation to executions, was that information given to you prior to your arrival at the site that you engaged in as an archaeologist?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think some information was given to me by the investigators at each site, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Is it fair to say then that prior to your arrival at each site, it was crystal clear in your mind that each time you were exhuming these graves that you were uncovering victims of mass executions? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not fair to say it was crystal clear in my mind. I regarded myself as a detached investigator in these matters, but I had some information given to me. In at least one instance, I also -- yes, I disagreed with the investigators as to the origin; for instance, Cancari Road 3, a secondary grave, I was told it came from one of the known execution sites and primary graves, and I said there must be another. Because of the contents of this grave, there must be another execution site or primary grave, which had not been found. It later was found. So I was not a pawn of the investigators, but I needed their advice to take me to the sites so I could prepare myself from the point of view of equipment and personnel for the sort of thing they expected to find.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Professor, I didn't mean to infer that you were somehow a pawn of the investigators here, but what I am suggesting or perhaps asking you is that in those graves where you found victims that weren't either blindfolded or ligatures?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Did it ever occur in your mind that the victims that you were uncovering may have sustained death as a result of conflict or combat? Did that ever come to the fore in your mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was thinking of all sorts of possibilities for these graves, that they might for instance date from the 1992 war and so on. We were always on the look-out for evidence that would test the propositions that had been put to me. I would not have been, I think, able to detect, with the knowledge I have, what you called combat casualties. I don't know how I, in my observations, would recognise that. That was the morgue's job to determine the cause and manner of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. You just indicated then about dating the grave sites. Was there a method employed at any of the sites that you were responsible for of dating the graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wouldn't technically be possible using the ordinary methods available to archaeology. The only way which, as I state in my reports, I list artefacts that were found in the grave, and many of those do provide links to Srebrenica, including news print from Dutch newspapers and the IDs which were subsequently examined in detail, but it was -- I -- had I seen evidence that was contrary to the advice of the investigators, we would have called a halt and had a conference, and I never had to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. You indicated yesterday that your role generally was to, as I understand it, and you will correct me if I've misinterpreted in any way, but, first of all, it was to extract artefacts which may have of assistance in identification of the victims. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sequence of my responsibilities was to precisely locate the grave, to excavate the grave, recover the bodies and put them into bags, and recover artefacts and put them into bags, and then the whole lot went down to the morgue for examination. But we formed, as it were, some contingency observations on the material, particularly on documents, because once reexposed to the atmosphere, they can start to decay; so we took photographs, but we were not studying them. My job was to get the bodies into the chiller vans and then they went down to the morgue with the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to take you to the -- I've just been suggested, Doctor -- Professor that we both slow down just for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: In relation to that role of artefact extraction, was there some check list or method that was employed at each of the sites in terms of what was deemed to be significant and what was not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's true to say that in the case of what I call the Srebrenica sites, all the artefacts were collected, and that would have included clothing, documents. The exception to this was the Cancari 3 site, where there were hundreds of thousands of pieces of broken glass and we just not collect them. We collected a sample. In general every artefact was, and logged, its location within the site surveyed, entered into the logs with a sequence number, and then packed away and sent down to the morgue. And that was the responsibility of the scene of crime officer to maintain custody of this material.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Can I take you to -- now, you provided, as I have photocopies of what seems to be two books of your working notes at the sites?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are -- these are my working notes. They're extracts from four books --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- relating to the investigations --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and these are very much my personal notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the material went into the logs and that was systematically recorded. These are observations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Observations.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Can I take you to I think, as I understand would appear in the first notebook at page -- you've numbered the pages at the top, and I read your writing as it seems to be page 68. Saturday 25 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, you have that there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, can you just perhaps -- I found your writing -- I'm not -- difficult to read. But can you just assist me there, is that an entry that does relate to assessment of items and identification of items?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It relates to the dam site and it relates to isolated items of clothing that were found in the refilling of the dam site.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right. And perhaps can you read out what exactly that entry says?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sorted cloth items into A, those that may aid identification photographed, have been photographed, itemized, logged, and retained. B, those that in our opinion would not aid in identification and have no evidential value were returned to the grave and a photo of the returned -- return taken. All shoes being retained for cleaning up."

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Just in relation to that second observation, can you tell me what criteria you adopted as to whether or not it would be relevant or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The criteria we generally use, and I think this was the only case where we didn't retain everything in the clothing, but hand-knitted sweaters, we would count as potentially identifiable items; but factory-produced jeans would be at the other end of the scale, they wouldn't -- without any names on them, they were unlikely to have been related to an individual; but potentially hand-knitted sweaters and any unusual jackets would have been thought to assist in identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And can I take you to page 206 of the same book. Do you have that there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, this is in relation to which site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: CR 12. That is the Cancari Road 12 site, I think. I must have a run back through.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will just need a moment to determine which site that refers to. The number you gave me what was, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: 206. Yes. It's CR 03, Cancari Road 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you've indicated at the bottom of that notation that there were was some clothing that was again deemed to not be relevant?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the -- just to check by reading the same page, I said, "Clothes of an approximately eight-year-old and approximately 12-year-old bones not associated," but they were not associated. Remember that site is a town rubbish dump. That was the primary site they were thinking was a town rubbish dump. I would have to look in the logs to see whether the clothing was retained, but I'm pretty certain it would have been. Not associated, doesn't mean we threw it out. It means there were bones of a young individual and there were some small clothes, but we couldn't actually say that the bones and the clothes came from the same individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So decisions were made at the sites as to what was considered relevant and what not. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's fair to say that sometimes those decisions were made.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you about your opinion as to whether certain sites could be interpreted as places of execution. All right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, you have been asked about this before in relation, particularly in relation to Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not I think yesterday as a place of execution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, but on prior -- in the Krstic trial, you were asked about this.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We -- are we talking about Kozluk, are we?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, I was. I'm sorry. I was thinking of another site. Yes, I was indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Now, your -- perhaps I'll ask you what was the basis upon which you made that assessment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis was that we found in the heap of bodies, those that were lying on the bottom, were in one case clutching a piece of vegetation that had its roots in the ground, that there were bullets embedded in the ground underneath some of the intact bodies that we uncovered, that at Kozluk something like 41 per cent had ligatures still attached. Fundamentally, it was that bullets were in the ground underneath these individuals who were lying flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And I assume that - perhaps you'll tell me otherwise - with the majority of the remains that you were dealing with here were skeletal or --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in Kozluk, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So there were some remains with soft tissue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were patchily distributed; but in the centre of the mass of bodies, oxygen doesn't get there and they putrefy very slowly; so on the edges there are skeletons, in the middle there is a lot of flesh.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, as I understand your evidence in Krstic, what you say is that on the fringes of the mass, you seem to be more confident in your assessment that those bodies had been shot where they lay; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, largely because they were lying on the ground, and we were able to use a metal detectors and determine that there were rifle bullets embedded in the soil underneath them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You have just indicated that those bodies -- I should say remains that were on the fringe were skeletal remains. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those that were right on the fringe, yes -- either that or they were mummified tissue. In all cases I think, except one at Kozluk, there was always some soft tissue there holding the bones together. But the -- the survival of soft tissue depends on being away from oxygen, and so that's why the ones in the middle of the heap are well preserved. And the ones on the bottom of those heaps, we were able to show had bullets embedded in the ground underneath them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. May I just clarify this with you then. Is it your evidence that as for the mass in the -- in the centre, the mass of bodies in the centre, you cannot be as confident that they were shot where they lay. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And as for the -- I think your expression was on the remains on the fringes you are 100 per cent confident or is it -- you -- that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would say, yes, I am 100 per cent confident that these people were -- when you say on the fringes, there is some continuity on the distribution. I would say that it never would have entered my head that they had not been shot on the spot there, and we the evidence of their being ligatured lying down and there were bullets underneath them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Just pardon me a moment, Professor. Now, there was -- you produced a diagram in relation to the distribution of bodies at Kozluk, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did in my report of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Could we perhaps have a look at P2177?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Counsel, please tell the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Sorry. P2177, as I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is that -- is that -- does that reflect what we're discussing in terms of the fringes and the mass?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects one of the sites which we labeled KK3. There is just along side, there is another, site KK2, where the execution evidence is also there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, perhaps if Madam Usher could assist the Professor, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps you could, with a marking, indicate, when we're being -- discussing what we define as the fringes, you could perhaps draw some boundary.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area that struck me in particular and that we studied in particular is this area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of this we interpreted as robbed. I can't recall whether these individuals in this area were -- had bullets underneath them, but this area I was personally present and studied in detail that I have marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And there is less -- now, are you able -- you are not able obviously to give any indication now as to whether or not they were bodies, the remains on the fringes were blindfolded or ligatured?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give that to you, but I would to go through the logs to give you that answer. If we look at KK2, there I know that the percentage of ligatured individuals, which I couldn't show you from my report if you don't have it handy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't -- at least one of the individuals in the upper area here is -- is clutching a shrub that was growing on the bottom, at the moment of death. The hand is tightly wrapped around it and that I interpreted as somebody clutching a -- a shrub at the moment of death, and I made -- gave some detail on that in my report, that particular individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Your -- in your opinion, though, your professional opinion, the fact that there were -- that these remains were interpreted by you as having been shot where they lay was not of itself an obstacle to any conclusion that they had been shot in the course of conflict, was it? Or combat?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer for all of them; but in the case of the one particular one that I illustrated in my report, I think it would be impossible to conclude that that person was shot in the course of combat, unless the combat was taking place on that site.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But again, pardon me, without being able to date, first of all -- and again I'm confining my comments to the remains where blindfold and ligatures are not found. Without being able to, first of all, date the remains and obviously date the presence of the bullets and the shell casings, you can't exclude that fact which you just raised?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're quite right. We're talking about Kozluk now. But in general, it's really exceptional that an execution site to get evidence of a death on the spot; and in most of the graves I was excavating, I couldn't say how the bodies had got into the graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you. I did comment in several of my reports that they had civilian clothing, but beyond that I could not determine how they died. I could determine that they had been dug up and put somewhere else, but you're quite right. It's not my field to determine whether people died in combat or --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Or executed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or executed. But at this site, I am totally confident as I am in grave L in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's where the 12 people were bound together with ligatures, and I won't ask you about that. All right. I want to ask you -- I don't need that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Actually, I will seek to tender that diagram, Your Honour, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be inserted in the system right away, and we will give it a number in due course when we come to the tendering process. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps he should initial it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Professor, could you please sign your name and give it a date, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll come to that later when we come to the tendering of documents stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Professor, I want to ask you about the question of engaging in an assessment of the age of any of these victims. Now, you -- is that something you simply didn't involve yourself with on -- on this site, that was a matter for the pathologist?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I ask you, do you mean the personal age of the individual at death or how old the graves are.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No the age of the individual at death?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't engage myself with that, except once as -- as in the case of that notebook entry about Cancari 3, I have anthropological knowledge. I wouldn't put myself forward as an expert but I made a note of that in my notebook, but that is a casual note off to at the side. The work is done at the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to ask you about this term of using a minimum number of persons. You're familiar with that in terms of an assessment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. You yourself didn't engage in that calculation --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- in relation to any of your sites. Were you, though, told at any stage by an anthropologist what the minimum number of persons was for each site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in my -- in my report on the field work of 1998, I mention the figures that I had been given by the morgue, and they were part of my report, as I gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Who -- can I ask you who the source of that information was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember offhand.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You can't.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's all right. Now, you did, however, engage in a mathematical calculation in relation to some unexhumed graves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, perhaps if you can assist the Trial Chamber in that -- in that regard.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I refer to my --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- notes on that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would like me to explain how I arrived at a number?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: This is the number of 2.571, first of all, perhaps if you could --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- explain that process which is --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the -- the argument that I put in my report runs like this, that we exhumed, totally exhumed seven secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I will just stop you. We better identify which ones those were.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were CR 3, CR 12, HZ03, HZ05, HZ04, LP02, and ZJ05. And the -- based on the morgue estimate of the number of individuals, that total 857.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We then tested at the surface to be sure that they were secondary graves; other graves that appeared on the same aerial imagery that we used and there were 21 of those that had multiple body parts, but which we did not exhume. On the assumption that they were at the same size, as the one we had already dug, which were themselves so similar to each other, I took an average of the number of individuals in the seven that we had dug, which was 122.4 in each grave, and I multiplied that up; and on the assumption that the other graves were typical of the ones we had dug, I came up with the possibility of there being -- a best estimate being 2571 -- 2571 for the probed but unexcavated graves. Then I added to those the actual number of bodies from the seven excavated graves which was 857, an estimate from the Red Dam of the minimum number of individuals, which I also got from the morgue, of 46. So I thought that the 1998 field season had probably accounted for some 3.474 individuals, assuming my assumptions were correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, this process in relation to the 21 assumed -- so the 21 graves that you used for the calculation, first of all, they are assumed to be secondary graves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're assumed to be secondary graves on the bases of the aerial imagery. They appeared at the same time as the one we exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. But you yourself have commented or noted that there are certain limitations on the use aerial imagery, is there not? In terms of locating individual sites?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we -- you must -- I didn't make it plain. These probed graves, we all located them as graves, but we just didn't excavate them. And we saw there were multiple body parts at the top, and we left them alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. But I'll get to the probing process in a moment. But just on the aerial imagery, generally what do you say about the reliability of aerial imagery reflecting accurately whether or not a grave is a secondary grave or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the aerial imagery doesn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only in the context of when those photographs were taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So once, having identified the areas in terms of the 21 graves, what was the -- was the first process that you engaged in the probing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the probing means that the backhoe -- sorry, I should say the excavator, which has a bucket with no teeth on it, scrapes the surface of the ground to find the edge of the grave; and then gradually a shallow trench is put in until we find that we find there are at least two individuals in the grave. That was all that we did, so as not to disturb the grave any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. So, first of all, as -- how do you -- how do you establish the perimeter of the grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows as a cut; that is, the filling of the grave is different in its colour, it is mottled. It's different in its colour from the natural soil into which it's dug. That's the fundamental way in which you detect a hole in the ground without disturbing what's underneath.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Is that different or that distinctive colour, is that the green/blue soil that occurs at the top which indicates decomposition of bodies? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be. But essentially in the type of soils that occur in Bosnia, you have a brown humic horizon near the top of the natural soil, and then you get down at about a metre to two metres down to a white-ish soil. So when you dig a grave, you bring up the material from below, and it gets mixed with the humus. You refill the hole, but the refilling of the hole is mottled with this white-ish soils from below and the darker soils from above. If the bodies are also very close to the surface, then you will get that greenish effect. But you can detect a grave, even though the bodies are two metres down.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this. On these occasions if you identified the body parts at -- I assume relatively close to the surface, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were in all -- in all instances close to the surface, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Can that process ever be deceptive in terms of the appearance of the soil, that if the grave has been dug up and emptied, the body -- there are simply no bodies in there any more, and the soil will still have that appearance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we don't stop -- that would happen, but we did not stop working until we had located at least two individuals within the grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. But let's say for argument's sake that at the superficial surface there are two individuals, but two metres down, as you -- which you did not --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't have to go far.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You didn't have to go that far, but you couldn't be obviously 100 per cent confident that there were no bodies beyond the two individuals that you found at the top?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No. Which is what I am getting at.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I wrote those assumptions in my account.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So in terms of these 21 graves, how many were you probing per -- can you -- as I read your report, it seemed like you would engage in this probing process on say three graves per day at one stage. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. We tended to do it in -- in batches, because we had to go out with a special team --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so we did batches of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was every three days, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would go out for a day or two and try to complete as much probing as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: In that day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that day, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What did you -- what did you mean -- I'm reading from an article that you wrote. This is fairly recently, 2005, The Archaeology of Mass Graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: At page 147 of that article, you've described the process of probing and say that "probing may be necessary in several areas since not all mass graves contain an even coverage of bodies?"

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: If the soil is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please slow down a little bit. For example, if you look at page 21, lines 6 and 7, we missed -- or the interpreters missed the witness's answer to your question, and also your next questions. So we could first cover that territory and then take either my advise to you to slow down. Your question was: "You didn't have to go that far, but you couldn't be obviously 100 per cent confident that there were no bodies beyond the two individuals at the top." And his answer was: "No, absolutely not." And then you said,-- which is missing here: "I was precisely coming to that," and I'm filling in these lapses --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- these blanks, actually. And he said: "Yes, and I wrote those assumptions in my account." But please slow down so that we don't have repetition of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just -- this is -- I think I was at the point of where you are indicating about probing may be ineffective if the soil was stoney, is that not the case here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And there you say, "Systematic probing is blindly destructive, and I may justify this, if information is urgently required for working out the logistics of forthcoming work." This probing of 21 graves in this period of time, that wasn't systematic probing at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what I meant by systematic probing, but in general -- well, I think I meant you shouldn't engage in this unless you need to. We wanted to know whether these other 21 graves that appeared on these photographs contained bodies or not, and that was the purpose of the word.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll ask you this then: Whose decision was it -- or at whose instruction were you asked to do the probing? Was it Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't operating under his instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ever. But I would have discussed it with him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, because he -- he's already given evidence in this Court, and he -- what -- he -- his assessment of his role was that he said -- this is at page 1548, where he says that his role was to identify the location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Pin-point them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in part.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah. Probe them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. If there is a statement of the witness, I think we should just hear it or allow him to see it in context as opposed to pick through it like that, if that's what indeed she's doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that's much important in this case. I think she's reading the relevant part, and she can then put the question. The whole purpose of her -- the exercise is to see whether there were overlapping responsibilities between the witness and Mr. Ruez, but I think the witness has already told you that --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- wasn't taking instructions from him. Now, if Mr. Ruez had any particular role in the digging process, perhaps you can put the question to the witness. But it would be a more pertinent question for Mr. Ruez himself when he returns. I think we can move through this very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps just let me ask you this, Professor, that Mr. Ruez was present at some of these 21 sites where you were engaged in the probing process. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether he was there when we were doing the probing at all. I wouldn't have expected him to be. I mean it was certainly not part of our protocol that he should be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And to tell you the truth, I can't remember whether he was there, though I did note in my notebooks at times who was there when we did the probing. But there was a very small team of experts who went out doing the probing, and we were not dependent on having Mr. Ruez there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you this then: When the decision not to exhume those graves, on what basis was that made?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Time and -- time and cost. We had run out of time by the end of 1998, and I wanted to get in each of the three roads; that is, the Cancari Road, the Hodzici Road, and Liplje Road. I wanted to get a sample of graves that were not -- that were well placed, evenly placed as possible down that road. I couldn't stick to that plan because some of the sites were unsuitable for us to get our equipment into, but I think I had what I would call a fair sample of the graves along each of the roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Just going back to that figure, the 2.000 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- 2.571 figure. Now, you would agree, wouldn't you, that there are quite a number of assumptions that you have taken into account in arriving at that figure?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah. And I -- in -- first of all, the most fundamental assumption is that there are in fact bodies under -- in the grave beyond the two that you found at the surface?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The fundamental assumption is that on average those 21 graves on average will reflect the average for the other --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Seven?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- graves that we dug, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Of course that involves the fundamental assumption that they're secondary graves and not primary graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Which we established at the outset, without a full exhumation you can't be 100 per cent sure; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That in the course of providing that figure to -- perhaps I should ask: Was that figure provided to Mr. Ruez originally or the Office of the Prosecution or --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that -- I did those calculations while I was writing my report after the field work had stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. At your own instigation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, we have problems once more. Please slow down and allow a short pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you ask me that question again before I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, if I can remember it. I was asking you just in relation to the calculations being at your own instigation, that figure.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And there is, of course, perhaps the most fundamental assumption in that figure that the bodies that you are assuming were there met their death in the course of an execution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- I don't think that's a necessary assumption on my part. My fundamental purpose is to see whether there are bodies in those graves, and how many. I'm not quite sure I understand the drift of your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Well, there -- there's another figure which you've added to that figure of 2.571, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. Because we get a total figure --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And what's the total figure that you have?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Total figure is 3.474, and that includes this extrapolation of 2.571 and the actual counts of 857 from the seven excavated graves, and 46 from the Red Dam.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So perhaps what I'm -- I'll be more explicit, Professor. What I'm getting is that when you provided the figure of 857, was that with a view to presenting that as evidence of victims that have been the subject of mass execution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's my duty to, I believe, find out how many bodies are in each grave and to report the evidence, but I don't see that the numbers, the numbers that are in the grave would be there regardless of how the people met their death. And that was the duty of the morgue to determine the manner and cause of death, though we obviously made observations at times, under critical circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: If you were to be -- err on the side of caution and be the most conservative as to what you could say about bodies that have been uncovered, you would no doubt use only the 857 figure and the 46 from Red Dam. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, because empirically, that's what I had. I should say though that I have been in touch with ICMP, who have now excavated many of these 21 graves. And I have asked them to let me know if there were any that were seriously empty, and they have told me that they all have bodies in them. And they are aware of my estimations, but I haven't personally studied that. It's word of mouth from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right. You are not, as a result of that, in a position to adjust that figure --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have regarded it as my professional responsibility to draw it to ICTY's attention if I was told that these graves were seriously empty. I was told they were fair, average qualities by somebody with me during the probing; that is, John Sterenberg of ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just one final issue that I want ask you about, Professor, and that is the determination between a primary grave and a secondary grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You've been asked before whether or not it's possible what's interpreted as a secondary grave is, in fact, primary grave into which bodies have been bulldozed and, therefore, bones torn apart.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found a primary grave with those properties, yes, at Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And if, in terms of the assessment of whether or not it's a primary grave or a secondary grave, you -- you found -- I mean the issue still remains, doesn't it, in relation to Zeleni Jadar, what the relevant primary grave is, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue doesn't remain in my mind, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right. Well, in terms of the location of the primary grave, though?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I concluded, as in my response to Mr. McCloskey yesterday, that I didn't have any doubt that the site of Glogova was the primary grave for Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. I misinterpreted your evidence in that regard. If you uncover a grave and the bodies are ostensibly or substantially complete, does that tend itself towards a conclusion that it's a primary grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is definitely a correlation there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Because just -- and this again appeared in your notes. Pardon me. This is in your second -- your second notebook that you provided, and at page 124. Do you have that? It has ZJ05 at the top?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have got that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So we're talking about Zeleni Jadar, and do you see there at the bottom that you do make the observation that bodies are relatively complete?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And then what's your further notation after that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "But tumbled," as in secondary burial.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right. All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meaning they're not lying flat, they're twisted around.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But just in terms of, again, leaving this matter open for interpretation, does -- does that initial assessment that the bodies are complete, does that make it open to interpret that it was, in fact, a primary grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just -- to explain what -- the way my mind runs on these things, imagine a heap of bodies that's been left out in the open for a long time at the spot, and then it's bulldozed into the grave some weeks later. The peri-ostial tissues that hold the bones together would weakened and bodies will come apart, and therefore that would be a trap for the unwary. But the reason for evaluating a grave as a secondary grave is not just the properties of the bodies, though they are correlated, it's also the importation of foreign matter into the grave, artefacts and soil and so on. But the state of the bodies on its own could lead to wrong conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You accept -- okay. And just -- let me put this to you, that if you didn't have the extraneous matter, the artefacts, foreign soil, to assist you in that assessment, and all you had was the state of the bodies, that that could therefore be the main indicator as to whether or not it was a primary or secondary grave?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to that. It is hypothetical. It is not reflecting the facts of case and therefore not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We fully agree with your object section, which is sustained. Move to the next question, please. I think he's answered the question in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, pardon me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Ms. Condon. Who is going next? Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, is it fair to say that part of your work was to find evidence that were in the soil and that were associated with the interred bodies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that soil residues or other materials that could be found on the bodies or on the clothing could reveal the place where the victims were killed or at least where they were before they died?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, particularly where they were buried before they were dug up and taken to the place of secondary burial, because that will transport the soil into which they were buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that with regard to the Glogova grave, you could establish a correlation between the victims buried in that grave and the Kravica warehouse precisely on account of some materials found in the grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Indeed, you went to the Kravica warehouse in order to check whether this type of materials could be found there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was -- that was what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you carry out similar examinations? Did you try to verify other locations where the victims could have been before they died? I'm not just speaking in relation to Glogova, this could apply to any grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The question of getting an expert to examine soil and vegetation arose in May 1998 at the Cancari Road site, that's Cancari 12. And Dr. Tony Brown, who is an expert in forensic vegetation and soil analysis, was -- was invited to come down to do just that, because it's outside my area of expertise. I can say, Look, in my view this soil should not be here in this secondary grave. But it's then handed over to him as a forensic expert in this matter, and he has written -- he has written reports for ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The event you are speaking about has to do with the soil analysis in a secondary grave with relation to the soil that would have been brought from the primary grave. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except that type of evidence of transfer of materials does normally apply to, in our work, to the secondary graves. But in the case of Glogova, we interpreted that as a primary grave, and Mr. Mike Hedley, who was a British police officer and was at Glogova when we excavated it, subsequently did a report on the material that I could only comment on it in an informal way. And I believe that report is part of ICTY's evidence, but I didn't take part in the writing of that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Precisely. I'll try to be clearer in the way I'm going to reformulate the question. Apart from Glogova where you could establish a connection with the Kravica warehouse, with regard to other primary graves, were you able to establish a connection with other sites or places where people would have been previously detained? Do you know for instance whether such examinations, soil analysis, were done in Bratunac, where there was the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. The only primary graves I was responsible for were the -- the Red Dam, and we saw nothing there that would suggest that sort of approach; and the -- the Kozluk site I excavated, that was a primary site, and there I determined that they -- so far as I could see, had been shot on the spot anyway. So the primary graves were not really my responsibility. I didn't see many of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to speak about a hole other than a grave that you found in Potocari. In your report of the 2nd of February, 1999 - for the transcript, this is P665, page 16 - you stated that you had found this hole in Potocari, but that you had not found any human remains. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was a hole that had been refilled and the soil didn't contain any human remains.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: However, what's written in your report, you saw -- you could see that the clay was blueish/greenish, that the soil was of that colour, which would show that this soil had been in contact with decomposing bodies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't, I think in my report, say that the soil was like that, but in the soil there were lumps of greenish clay, and that greenish clay is of the type that forms around bodies. But I have to say it's not just human bodies, around animal bodies, so it's not diagnostic of a human burial site.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Indeed. Well, you anticipated my next question. On the basis of what you could see in the soil, you could not establish whether the changes in colour were due to human or animal remains?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I regarded that as a totally unsatisfactory site from the point of view of saying that it had anything to do with human remains. That is my archaeological view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there has been a shred of evidence that would indicate that elements were dug up. Just be aware that we are losing time on such questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Mr. President. I just wanted to seek some clarification. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Who is next? Who would like to go next? Yes, Mr. Ostojic. You had indicated about 45 minutes. Do you stick to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You require more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a break in about nine minutes' time

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, good morning.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a couple of questions. I hope not to be repetitive. I do not believe I will be. Sir, I would like to start by asking to you give me the complete definition of the archaeological use of the word "artefact"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the history of archaeology, archaeologists had to distinguish between natural objects in the soil and humanly manufactured and modified objects in the soil, and the latter were called artefacts so that it covers the whole range of material, in the forensic case from clothing to bullets to glass. It's -- it's anything made or modified by humans.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And other things like a personal identification cards or any personal belongings on a person as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an artefact; and as was recorded, they were all recorded with an A in front of them on our logs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I saw that. Thank you. Let me understand the process. There were essentially three experts, if you will, that participated in the exhumation process involving Srebrenica; the archaeologists, which is your field, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then the anthropologist, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There wasn't an anthropologist at -- at -- in the sites, who was in the same way as myself the chief anthropologist. There were anthropologists who were working under my direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, okay. And we'll get to that specifically, but my question is of the three areas of expertise, if you will, was yours, the archaeologist, then there is the anthropologist, and then the pathologist, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The pathologist are not at the site, if you're talking about the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about generally.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, generally. Yes, then that's another matter. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am talking about generally involving the exhumation process of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. As Mr. Mrkic is rightly pointing out to you, Mr. Ostojic, once more you are going too fast. Please slow down. It is for your own benefit at the end of the day because you get a transcript missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I need -- I think you need to go through it again. His last recorded answer was: "No. The pathologist are not at the site, if you're talking about the site." And then you said, "I'm talking about generally." And he said, "Oh, generally. Yes, then that's another matter." And we can continue from there now. So I think the missing piece has been filled by myself and we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So am I correct, those are the three areas of expertise?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you define for me if there was any overlap with respect to the expertise of any of these three specific areas?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean whether some people worked -- yes. There is overlap. For instance, I have expertise in anthropology, but I don't count myself as an expert. Most of the archaeologists, I would say all of the archaeologists working under my direction had knowledge of human osteology. So there is overlap in expertise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In connection with your report, did you utilise the expertise of the other two expert areas that we discussed; namely, pathology and anthropology?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the anthropology, as I explained in the previous answers, to -- I used the anthropologists to determine the minimum number of individuals and they did that in the morgue, but I don't recall feeding back into my reports any information from the pathologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember or if you can tell us if you ever worked with an anthropologists called David Del Pino, a Chilean anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think I have, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You worked with Dr. Clark, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say worked with, he was working in the morgue as the same time as I was working at the sites, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Other than that, did you not coordinate your efforts between Dr. Clark, the pathologist, while he was the chief pathologist?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Clark, on at least two occasions, came to the excavation sites to see how we were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So I understand the bigger picture here, you mentioned that you were involved in digging, as I think you used, or exhuming two primary grave sites, and can you tell us then how many secondary grave sites you were involved in during the course of 1998 through 2001, which I believe is the time period that you worked?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1998, I examined two primary graves and seven secondary graves. In 1999, for the purposes of this project, I examined Kozluk which was a primary grave; in 2000, I examined Glogova. So those two primary sites need to be added to the figures that I've already given you. But as I've explained yesterday, I was doing a lot of other work for ICTY as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm just trying to get a bigger picture. Just tell me, was it four primary sites that you were involved in exhuming and two secondary sites or what is the total number for each?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be four primary sites and seven secondary sites by the time I finished in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is it fair to say, sir, that it is important with respect to the artefacts that are found in these primary and secondary sites that they are important evidentiary matters that should be retained?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fundamentally, yes. The problem comes in applying that rule to bodies that have been buried for example in town rubbish dumps because then you are faced with thousands of artefacts that probably don't have any relation to the manner and cause of death or identification. But in general, where the task is manageable within the resources available, yes, we would log all the artefacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you would attempt to do in a most thorough and complete manner, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was that as soon as an artefact was found the scene of crime officer would allocate it a number in the log, it was handed to him. After its location in the site had been surveyed by the three -- using three-dimensional coordinates. And then the scene of crime officer takes custody of that object. That's the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who is the crime scene officer who was in charge and handled that chain of custody for the primary and secondary graves that you were exhuming?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They varied. Police from various police forces were provided to me. But in 2000 I had the advantage of a scene of crime officer for the whole season.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you just briefly describe for me what the role of -- or who is the forensic anthropologist who assisted you in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were several forensic on the pathologists. Their names are in the front of the book, but they were -- they were selected because they had mixed capabilities in archaeology and anthropology at the site. Down at the morgue I think that Mr. Jose-Pablo Baraybar was in charge of the anthropology for the most of the time, but I wasn't down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Given the importance of retaining and maintaining these artefacts, would I be correct to say that it would be inappropriate or improper to do a cursory review of such artefacts as opposed to a thorough and complete review?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I mean, the investigators were responsible for that and I didn't see the type of review they did, but I would hope that they did a thorough review, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Should we have a break. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'm going to try to cut to the chase a little bit in the interests of time. Sir, with all due respect, I suggest to you that based on your reports that your team, which include the scene of crime officers, the anthropologists and archaeologists and all the investigators, that in fact you did an inappropriate and improper review of the artefacts.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did a contingency review of the artefacts. I don't believe any of the comments I made were improper and all of them assumed that further study would be done by the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am suggesting, sir, that in fact, it was not done thoroughly and it was not done completely, but it was actually done as a -- on a cursory basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the -- speaking of his review or the investigative review, it's unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Instead of ruling on the objection itself, perhaps you can rephrase, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You heard my learned friend's objection. I am interested in both, both yours and the rest of the team, Professor. I am suggesting that both your review and examination of those artefacts were inappropriate and incomplete?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My review was incomplete, but I don't understand -- deny that it was inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, how about the rest of the team, would you also agree with me that that was incomplete?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rest -- what do you mean by the rest of the team?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, if you look at your report, you listed out who other members of the team are: For example, staff members of the ICTY; for example, the scene of crime officers that you mentioned, both from Britain and the police forces; the contracted archaeologists and anthropologists that you list, including I believe your wife, Sonja Wright, correct? She worked with you on some of these?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she worked with me for many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand. So listing all those 22 names, that's who I'm referring to, that anybody who worked with the artefacts actually did an incomplete job and merely did a cursory job of both the collection and the examination of those artefacts. I'm correct, aren't I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are presenting a compound question, because "incomplete" is one way of projecting it, or proposing it; "cursory job" is another. If you mean to say or to put to the witness that it is incomplete because it was cursory, then please put the question in that manner. If you -- if you want to put to the witness that it was both incomplete and cursory, then you need to put it clearly so. And, again, I think that we need to keep separate the stages that Mr. McCloskey pointed out when I asked you to rephrase your question, because the report is his, and not necessarily of the members of the team that were working with him or under his direction. So I know for sure that you are understanding what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need -- I'm not stopping you in any way. I'm just asking you to be more articulate and to put precise questions to the witness, because he's already said, for example, "I agree with you that it was incomplete." But if the suggestion is or was that it was incomplete because it was a cursory, then I would suggest that we go back to the same question and ask the professor to explain to us why he agrees with you that his exercise was incomplete exercise or examination of the artefacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'm not arguing with Mr. President or the Trial Chamber, but I think the professor actually answered that right before the break on page 39, when I asked him specifically on lines 13 through 15, whether it would be inappropriate and improper to do a cursory review, and his answer, which appears on line 16, he says, "Well yes," and then he continues. I thought I established that already, but I will take the question as Mr. President suggests. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, you heard the exchange, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you comment on that? Was it incomplete because it was cursory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said it was incomplete, it's incomplete because I know that the investigators will be doing a thorough and complete job later. But I wish to include in my report certain observations as I have made, and I would not be using a word -- the word "incomplete" or I think even "cursory" in a pejorative manner, maybe a statement of the detail which I went into because I knew it was going to be followed up at the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you ever obtain from these scene of crime officers or from anyone this report which would indicate to us whether or not it may or may not be complete, the collection and examination of the artefacts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't -- I haven't had such reports referred to me. I don't know whether they were done or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So as you sit here now, based on -- sorry, I thought they were asking me to slow down. I apologise. So as you sit here now, sir, you have never, to this date, based on any of the exhumations that you have conducted, received a report from any scene of crime officer or ICTY investigator to confirm your premises or your assumption, if you will, that these artefacts and the examination of these artefacts would be done in a thorough and complete manner. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not been -- I was on a contract to carry out the excavations and write a report on the excavations. I had not overall responsibilities for the case as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, because Mr. -- The Honourable Mr. President wanted me to clarify this. Your report, and I have read it, the summary findings uses the plural "we" when you wrote this report. And can you describe or tell me who you meant when you said "we" in certain aspects of the report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would have to specify what.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at your summary findings, the very first report from February 1999, I believe. Oh, I'm sorry, May 12th, 1999. Sorry. Do you have that in front of you, possibly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll just take a look at page 2 there, and I think that's where it starts with the summary findings in bold.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
