utterances.text: Okay. The sixth paragraph below, do you see that, where you start the sentence, "We"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Who are you referencing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's used in the collective sense of the team that we were -- that I was working with a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. And I think you list, in that very report on the very next page, page 3 and page 4, who the members of the team were. You said that there is an ICTY investigator, that there as both the Dutch and the British scene of crime officers, there's the archaeologists and anthropologists, 22 or so members; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So that is who you were referring to. This report is written on behalf of those people as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not written on behalf of them, but the "we" merely indicates that I am not alone in doing the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's read the sentence that starts with "we". It states, "We carried out only a cursory examination of artefacts found in the graves." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell me what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is that the artefacts such as the identification documents, the writings, require analysis beyond that which we are capable of; that's one thing. The second thing is that we did not do invasive analysis of the bodies to see what might be inside inner pockets, so it was cursory in the sense that we did not attempt to recover all the artefacts. And for me to have claimed not -- for me not to have qualified my statement on the artefacts would have been, I think, irresponsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about whether or not before you were contracted by the Office of the Prosecution to conduct these exhumations whether you were familiar with criticisms of prior archaeologists or anthropologists in conducting exhumations in connection with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in a -- when I was interviewed at ICTY in 1997, it was made plain to me that they -- they wanted, for the 1997 season, somebody with extensive archaeological experience, and that is why they were selecting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you ever informed, sir, that there was ever a problem at least cited by not just one Chilean anthropologist, but other anthropologists that there were directions given to the staff members working in the exhumation process to discard clothing and to throw away certain artefacts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not those details, I was not told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And to this day, sir, is your testimony that you are unaware of such conduct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am of very vague word of mouth criticisms of -- of work in 1996 that some archaeological procedures were not -- not exact, and that ICTY in 1997 decided to get a full-time archaeologist to conduct the exhumations. But the details of what had worried ICTY, if indeed ICTY was worried, no, they were not part of my briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you mention that from time to time during the process of conducting these exhumations that you were informed by ICTY or Office of the Prosecutor investigators as to the -- some factual back drop of some various sites. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed what they believed the sites represented, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the ICTY investigator, and I think through my learned friend from the Defence, you said you mentioned -- or she mentioned Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically him and others, those that you may have been in contact with, such as Dean Manning other others, did they ever inform you as to why you did not find any military clothing in any of the graves that you exhumed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I asked them. I don't remember that -- my -- there was my statement that -- my observations that we had not found military clothing, but I don't remember having it explained to me as to why we hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you ever informed that the men that left Potocari in July of 1995 was a military column at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I may have read that, but it was not a point of -- in background, yes. But I don't remember it being -- I don't remember being instructed on such matters, if you know what I mean. All sorts of conversation goes on at the site and so on, but I was not formally -- I was not formally told or instructed on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, help me with this then: What is the significance of noting what the type of clothing is on these graves that you have exhumed --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- if not to suggest that they were civilians versus military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So. If you are basing it, and the reason you're putting this information is to do what, confirm if you will, that these were non-military people?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's to point out that I did not find any military clothing, because I thought it was my duty to describe the -- the general nature of what I was finding in my reports. But I was certainly -- I was certainly away of the -- of the significance of my observations in the context of what people believed military, non-military possibilities for these graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, would it impact your decision -- your opinion or any of your reports if I would suggest to you that the Prosecutor has also identified this column of men leaving Potocari going to Tuzla as being a military column?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have told, apart from the fact that people were wearing civilian clothing, what the background of these people was. It wouldn't -- I don't see what it would impact. I made the statement that there was no -- there were no items of military clothing observed by me, but that the final decision on that would have to be made at the morgue when things were cleaned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, we discussed briefly these calculations that you made, I think, in May of 1999, and I know that were -- and I think you responded in a report once it was -- with all due respect, I think there was a criticism raised with respect to your calculations being assertions as opposed to assumptions, and I think you clarified that in a memo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- my calculations are not assumptions, but the -- the interpretation you place on the calculations require some assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, and I think in -- that's the memo that you wrote to my learned friend Peter McCloskey in November of 2000, correct? You're familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that one, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have it with you, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have that one with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's -- I have the ERN number. It's -- just for the record, I'll just place it on the -- 0106-2373 dated the 13th of November, 2000, to Peter McCloskey from Richard Wright.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, in part of this, and I'll quote what you say, "I agree that the exact number can only be determined by actual exhumation. That inferences require assumptions and I have not argued otherwise in my report." Now, to date, sir, do you agree with that still today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To date, sir, do you know what the actual exhumation or, if you will with all due respect, body count is from the exhumations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the exhumations that I was working with or all the exhumations that have ever taken place?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All of them that have ever taken place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever seek to learn that information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sought to learn, as I explained to your colleague earlier, I sought to learn from Mr. John Sterenberg of ICMP and I asked him to tell me, when they excavated these secondary graves that are used in my calculations, whether any of them would undermine the calculations that I did, and he assured me that they didn't; in other words, they were fair, average quality graves in terms of numbers of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At the time that you made those calculations, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is this year, these year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you speak with Mr. Jean Ruez, and did you give you his assessment as to the percentage of graves that were exhumed to date?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I speak with him when?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time since your reports.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- can you just rephrase what it is that would you like know that I spoke about?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: First, I want to establish whether you did speak about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have spoken to Mr. Ruez many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When was the last time, for example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time was in 2002 at a conference in Bournemouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And for four or five years you haven't spoken to him at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not since 2002, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his opinion was in 2002 as to the number of graves that you were exhumed relating to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did he ever discuss with you that at that time it was his opinion that 94, 95 per cent of the graves were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That is a misstatements of facts. This was not brought up when Mr. Ruez was here, and I think it's incumbent on counsel when he has an issue to have at least cross-examined Mr. Ruez on that point, though that's not the foundation of my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, please respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, I actually did cross-examine him and I read it yesterday, and it was Mr. Ruez who gave us those percentages. It was based on his opinion, based on all the work that he has done as the lead investigator, as he identified himself being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you recall the answer that we heard was not the percentage of exhumed but the percentage of identified, and that is a -- quite a bit -- big difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We do have an idea, but rather than risk relying on our memory, or our respective memories, Mr. Ostojic, perhaps you could go straight to chapter and verse and read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. It was on -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. On page 1731, and I'm reading from yesterday's transcript which appears on page 42, starting on line 25 and proceeding on page 43 line 1 through approximately 12, and I state in -- I read from page 1731 of Mr. Ruez's testimony. "I was asked in 2003, line 3 and on. 'In 2003, isn't it correct that was your opinion with respect to exhumations,'" and I'm stressing it, obviously. "You said, 'We are now in 2003. Eight years after the events. We have located probably 90 per cent of all these graves.'" . Then I proceed, "'Do you remember giving this statement in the Blagojevic case, page...'" and they didn't write it down, because I was perhaps speaking fast, "'line'" blank through line 12. Answer, but Mr. Ruez, again, they didn't say it, but I think it was "Yes," but we can check that. Question: "'Now we are even more removed'" from the dates . "'Yes,'" answer. "'What per cent does it increase or decrease that I can use?'" "'Only one site has been found since 1993. It is a site located in Potocari that was discovered by the team of Mr. Masovic. This is so maybe we are now at 96 per cent.'".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is hard to -- to gauge hearsay of a previous statement, but Mr. Ruez appears to be talking about graves that were located, located, and that another one had been located in Potocari. It's a -- well, I won't get into anything besides that. He's talking about locating graves, not -- not digging them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he -- I appreciate that, and I guess he could change his position from first I identifying bodies to locating graves. I truly believe the evidence is quite clear, especially given Dr. Clark's testimony yesterday as to the number of bodies and looking at Professor Wright's testimony today in his report on what his extrapolations were. Putting that in context with Mr. Ruez, which is quite clear, despite my learned friend's perhaps attempt to recreate what he said, I think it's pretty obvious what it is. He says there are 96 per cent that have been exhumed. Graves. Mr. Ruez mentions graves. He's not talking about identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will strongly object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. McCloskey, I interrupted you when you had just said, "I will strongly object to that." Can you explain again your objection, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The statement that 96 per cent of the graves had been exhumed, and that is nowhere in this record. It misstates the actual reality of the day as we sit here, and that Mr. Ruez and anyone in this field full knows well that there are many, many graves left unexhumed in this -- in this case. And to suggest that the record suggests that 96 per cent is -- is absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic. Let's cut to --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we will, but I do strenuously object. Not because -- I mean but these are comments -- if he wants to make an argument, my learned friend, he can make one; and if he thinks he has a basis for it, he can do so. I have to say this for the record and, apologise, Mr. President. All they ever say is that we're wrong. All they ever say is it's not true. I would like him to show me where his report is to indicate and which report specifically tells us how many graves reportedly are still left that need to be exhumed. And I want him to tell us specifically, when he has evidence like this, why they didn't withdraw draw such evidence when it goes contrary to what Dr. Clark said given what he said yesterday about the number of bodies and body parts that he actually examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think you need to rephrase or reput your question, and I'm pretty sure that Professor Wright knows exactly what you are talking about. And if he is in a position to answer your question, he will do so; if not, we will move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you know what the percentage of the graves that relate to Srebrenica, do you know how many have been exhumed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever ask the Prosecutor to provide you with that information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask the Prosecutor to provide me with that information. The background of my work is that I stopped working for ICTY in 2000. I've moved on to other jobs. I have written my reports. I don't have an overarching responsibility to follow this material up, but I have asked people to let me know if there are any matters relating to my work, which are -- must be re-examined. They have not told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me why the Office of the Prosecutor, if it's true that there are other graves that need to be exhumed, do you know if they've ever informed you who is conducting any of those exhumations currently?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that, because I've been in touch with Mr. John Sterenberg, who was working with me all the four years I was in Bosnia, and he is the field officer for ICMP. And he informs me periodically of this work but on an informal bases and nothing alerted me to the possibility that we had misled the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure why you're continuously referencing misleading the ICTY or anyone, but we can talk about that at some other time. My point is this: Your friend that you keep in contact with, who is continuing these exhumations, can you tell us based on your formal or informal conversations with him, when was the last time an exhumation was conducted on a grave relating to Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm confident that they were conducted right up to the autumn of last year. They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know prior to that how many, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many graves were exhumed since you left the Office of the Prosecution in your role as the chief archaeologist, sorry?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't answer that question. I -- I was not a part of the system, as it were, after 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. But you do agree with me, sir, though that the exact number, when determining bodies and the number of bodies that were recovered from graves that were exhumed, would you agree with me that that body count, if you will, is best left for a pathologist like Dr. Clark, who you worked with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the anthropologist and pathologist team, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you this about the secondary and primary graves, and you've helped me identify exactly that and the numbers that you've looked at. And this is a little tricky, but I'm trying to get the question right. I believe, from reading your reports, there was one exhumation that you conducted on a secondary grave, and then you determined subsequent to that exhumation that it related to another primary grave. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, yes. I think you're referring to the relationship between Zeleni Jadar 5 and the Glogova site.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm referring to, and thank you for clarifying that it's Zeleni Jadar 5 and the Glogova site. Which Glogova site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked on what was called Glogova 1. I did not see any of the exhumations that took place at Glogova 2. They were conducted under Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any time, during your experience with the exhumation, conduct any other similar types of exhumations where you first found the secondary grave site and then subsequent to that found the primary grave site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The third site in Cancari Road had properties of broken bottles, and the broken bottles suggested to me that there must have been some industrial accident at a bottling factory. And that was when I contacted ICTY to tell them that I believe there must be a primary grave associated with the bottling factory at Kozluk, because that's what the labels were telling us -- I mean, Kozluk was mentioned on the labels we were finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Those were glass bottles, right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We found that -- the point is that the glass bottles were broken but they still had the Crown seals on them; that's not what you expect from discarded picnic rubbish. The labels were not stuck on the bottles. So I thought there was a moment in the production process where a large crate of bottles, that had been sealed but not labelled, had broken and they had been dumped, and that the bodies were with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any others other than those two that you have just mentioned, where you found first a secondary grave site and then subsequent to that you found the primary grave site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, just a follow-up question from page 47 today, lines 12 through 14 - and we're only saying that for the record, so I don't that you will find it in front of you - we talked about the significance of your observations in the context of what people believed were military or non-military clothing. Can you tell me, as you sit here now, whether or not your statements in your reports that you found no military clothing or the converse, that you found only civilian clothing, can you tell me what significance, if any, does it have in your reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we had found no military clothing, we -- I included in my 1998 report and in my 1999 report. But in Glogova in my report, that's there is mention of a possibility military jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of one, and I think you found that the button was actually commercially made, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a different find.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Different one?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the jacket was so dirty that it would have to be checked in the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What's the significance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance is I am aware of the possibility...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of the general background of argument that are these soldiers or are they civilians, but I mean you couldn't work in Bosnia without that being -- hearing that discussed. I was impressed with the fact that I was seeing people who had only civilian clothing on with that one exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with military personnel wearing civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever inquire of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't inquire of that fact. I think I was told that some of the people who -- some of the people changed into civilian clothing, but these are talk that one hears and I didn't inquire into it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's all the questions I have. Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. The Nikolic team, you had indicated ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Madam Nikolic. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's going to take literally one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Professor. I'm going to put a question to you that relates exclusively to your methodological approach in your work. When you were calculating the number of bodies in the graves and this number, 2.571, that is the total number, you said that this was an assumption. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are assumptions underlying that number, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a scientist can you please tell me if you agree that in the scientific or methodological method, an assumption is a claim that should be proved and it should not be something that is found in conclusions in any case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that in the case of scientific method, it's pointless to make assumptions that can't be tested. Now, I knew that the assumptions I was making could be tested by further exhumation. And I, therefore, did not regard it as scientifically irresponsible to do these calculations and to set out the assumptions underlying them because, I knew that the hypothesis I was putting forward could be tested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you entirely; but until there is confirmation, it remains in the domain of an assumption, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It remains perhaps in the domain of a hypothesis, yes, with assumptions underlying it, but I am not suggesting -- I did not propose that that is the number. I was saying that that would be the number if certain assumptions were met of the similarity between the grave we dug and the graves that remained undug.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, sir. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. I have an indication that the Gvero Defence team doesn't wish to cross-examine the witness. Can I have an confirmation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have that confirmation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. That leaves you, Mr. Haynes or Mr. Sarapa. You indicated 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I should comfortably finish within that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Professor, I wonder whether you would consider a couple of statements and see whether you agree with me. Forensic archaeology is concerned with the understand of activities from the past and the investigation of physical remains whether they are objects, corpses, or residues.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that general statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And forensic anthropology is the application of the science of physical anthropology and human osteology in a legal setting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that seems a good summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Putting it simply, as an archaeologist, you look at what is in the ground and how it got there; and an anthropologist looks at who's there, what they are, and how many there are?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I would say yes to that question, it would imply that I don't believe there is a crossing between the practices of the two subjects. But in the sense that one is acting as archaeologist, yes and one is acting as an anthropologist, yes, and we had specialist in both fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I commend your honesty, but are in fact an emeritus professor of anthropology at Sydney University, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is why I explained yesterday the confusion of terminology, in that in this context anthropology was osteology. At Sydney University, anthropology is -- was used in its old sense of covering prehistoric archaeology, physical anthropology, and cultural anthropology. And so there were two professors of anthropology, one of them being myself for a time, and we had -- I had the responsibility to deal with the archaeological side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have only put these questions to you in case you feel uncomfortable answering questions about anthropology, which I'm going to ask you. I assume you feel comfortable answering questions about anthropology?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have practiced not in the context of this work, but in other forensic cases, a consider amount of anthropology myself, so I should feel comfortable, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In order to determine the age, sex, race, and minimum number of individuals in a grave, the standard technique involves, where you can't complete a skeleton, looking at bone growth and age-induced change, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does, as well as dental eruption stage and the degree of wear on the teeth. But -- if I add that into what you said, yes, I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in your considerable experience, you presumably agree that any assessment of the contents of the grave requires, as it were, a controlled sample? I can put that better, if you don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, what I was going to say was that every grave we examined, we were charged with removing all the individuals within the grave, so we were not sampling.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I didn't put that well. There are racial variations to bone growth and age-induced change, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very much. In -- most of the racial differences relate to the cranial form; but in the post-cranial skeleton, there's not much different between people all over the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I mean, just to quote an obvious example, you have just been cross-examined by Mr. Ostojic, who is from America, and I am from the United Kingdom, and would you agree that, as it were, a control sample of Americans wouldn't be of much use in determining the age of those dug up in Europe?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean age of death?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I would race into agreeing with you on that, no. I would like to see local studies done, but the general principles that are set out in anthropology text-books, except for certain aspects of cranial variation, have always suggested to me a fairly uniform process of growth in the human species.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. I think we're going to have to agree to disagree on that one. It's also true, isn't it, that practicing as an anthropologist you have to be very careful of the ethics of what you do? And in particular in the removal of human remains from grave sites?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, presumably, you would agree that, in the work that was carried out in Bosnia, researchers should have obtained the informed consent of any persons they intended to study?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. The relevancy of this line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Move to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There is no next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that leaves us with the possibility of a re-examination on your part, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A couple of points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Professor, I want to take you back to the Kozluk grave very briefly, and I would like to go to a couple of pages of your report, if you could help us illustrate a point that you were making on cross-examination. And it's 65 ter 665. It's page 27 of your report of 2nd February 2000, and we should get it up on the screen. As it's coming up, let me ask you, you found that -- that site at Kozluk roughly about the same time the investigators did. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it before the investigators, but I went there with the investigators. I found it because of the properties of Cancari 3, but physically I went there with the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see any shell casings in the area of the -- of the excavation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At Kozluk, yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they are mapped in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We talked about bullets you found in the grave underneath bodies. Did those shell casings that you found relate to the -- to the bullets in any way? Do you know if they were the same size or is that not something that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not something that -- I knew that the material was going to be handed over to a ballistics expert, but they didn't look as though -- they didn't look as though they didn't fit, if you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the amount of shell casings lead you to come to any conclusions or was it -- did it fit into your view-point of that grave at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was not just the amount, but the distribution of the shell casings. The shell casings were under the bodies in many instances. They were everywhere, the shell casings. There were hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if you can look at this photograph, and do you recognise where that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Kozluk site, and it's what we called KK2. It was a distribution of bodies just at the side of the one that we were seeing illustrations of earlier in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall if any of those bodies appeared to have been shot in situ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the ones that I was referring to lying on a surface with many bullets in the ground surface beneath them. I had a pen and I lost it. Can I point? Does it show up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The usher will help you out with that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would it be possible to show parts of both photos, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: To slide it up the screen slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could see if we can get a bit of both in there.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's enough. That's fine, thank you. No, the previous size was better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think more space.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. These are individuals that I concluded were -- were shot on the spot. They lay on this surface, and there were bullets in the ground underneath them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't you -- could you put an X by the individuals you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all these individuals, including some probably not included slightly to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, in the lower photograph, you can see all of them in a slightly different angle. The green suit and then across to the left there are some missing in the upper photograph, but it's a photograph of the same distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And something I think we talked about very briefly about yesterday, I asked you how you could tell from digging, excavating a grave, whether something had been disturbed or not. Can you tell us about those markings in the bottom of the -- the bottom picture?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the -- when an excavator digs into clay, it compresses the clay and the softer material that's put above doesn't obliterate the marks of an excavator. And this is -- these are the marks of an excavator that came later than the disposal of the remains, because it cuts across the legs of an individual who is on the slope with the rest, and the leg is gone. And we interpret this as the robbing of a grave area at Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you mark with an L where the leg is gone, if you can recognise it from that picture?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a diagram in my report which shows this more clearly, but it's in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So these -- these scratches in the lower photograph, those are not scratches your excavation made?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the bodies that are in these photographs, is that the precisely the way they were in when you found them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were underneath about up to a metre of soil, which had been thrown in some manner on to that surface and covering the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you and your experts were able to take all the soil off and leave that -- leave that just the way they were when they died --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- in your view. Let's take a look at one more page, and that is -- yeah, sorry. We need to have you sign this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we proceed, if the witness could sign over this document and date it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour, unless the Court finds it significant, we do have the report. I think it,-- with all due respect, may be outside the scope of the cross-examination, and my learned friend did mention that he was referring to his direct yesterday in trying to supplement it. And I understand that it's significance, and you know we may want to look at it, but we do have those reports. If he wanted to lead him with that evidence, he should have yesterday. I don't believe that anybody touched on these pictures today, and it is strictly outside the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is your response to that, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Condon cross-examined very seriously on Kozluk on the question of whether or not the people had been shot at this place, and as this Court knows, there is no survivor of that execution. Therefore, I am just clarifying, with the evidence to back up, what his conclusions were; that people did in fact were in fact shot there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We agree with you, Mr. McCloskey. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could now go to the last photograph, 65 ter 665. It's page 29 of the -- of the same report. There's two photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned in your -- I believe it was your cross-examination that one of the reasons you based your opinion on people being shot there was a person had grasped some -- some plants in the grave, and I wanted, if you can, is this exhibit what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And looking at that lower photo, were you able to determine that those plants actually had been rooted into the soil?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were now dead, but they had been rooted into the soil. They had been covered up of course by --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, professor. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that we have the correct reference for these two pictures. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could mark that again, thank you for -- before we close it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think there is a need to mark it, actually because you just referred --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's why I didn't mark it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to enter this into the record or we'll have one page less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had meant earlier on to put a series of questions to you, which however Mr. Haynes covered. There is only one thing that I would like you to clarify for us, Professor. I have understood the interrelationship that exists particularly in University Sydney, when it comes to archaeology, anthropology, et cetera. What I would like you to clarify is the following, especially since you said that in other instances you also played a role -- or filled the role of an anthropologist proper. In this particular assignment that you had on behalf of the ICTY, not just one but more than one, did you restrict your role to that of an archaeologist proper, or did you also at times fill the role of an anthropologist, too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never filled the role of an anthropologist in the sense that I worked at the morgue, but I noticed some very clear observations on bones, such as an immature individual, and I made a note in my notebook. It is passed. The whole matter is passed to the morgue for the anthropologists; nothing was left with me to determine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Professor. We have come to the end of your testimony. You will receive the assistance you require, and I wish to thank you on behalf of the Tribunal, and also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Meek. In relation to the tendering of documents, are there any documents to be tendered or have they all been tendered before, pursuant to our previous decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Been -- Your Honour, Mr. President, they have been tendered before, or they are already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Except with the one that you have made use of now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which will be marked accordingly. Are there any objections to its admission. I am referring to the two photos -- all right. Thank you. Do any of the Defence teams wish to tender any documents. I hear -- yes, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You made reference to several articles.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I put P 2177 to the professor and that was the document that he marked with the red pen, so I would seek to tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any objection on your part, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. It is so admitted. No further -- you don't intend to tender the articles that you referred --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the witness to? All right. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if it please the Court, I have some business. I need to leave now. My client has approved that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you so much, Mr. Meek. Now, next witness. Who will be handling the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is here and ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could leave for one second, if I could be right back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. McCloskey. Good morning, Dr. Lawrence, and welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence. Let's go through the solemn declaration procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Dr. Lawrence. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Rupert Elderkin from the Office of the Prosecutor will be examining you in chief. He will then be followed by some or more of the -- some or all of the members of the Defence teams. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Examination by Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I start by asking you to say your name, please?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Christopher Hamilton Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Dr. Lawrence, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I am a forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where are you currently working?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I am the State Forensic Pathologist for Tazmania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what you do day-to-day in that job?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: As the state forensic pathologist, I am responsible for providing the autopsy service for the coroner in Tazmania, that involves examining deaths, trying to establish how the deaths occurred, examine the injuries, and try and formulate opinions about the circumstances in which the death occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that you have some training also in anthropology. Could you describe the extent of that, please?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: My principal training is in forensic pathology, but I have attended a number of courses. I spent two years working in the United States; and during that time, I attended two courses in forensic anthropology. I've also attended a number of courses subsequently. I've also performed examinations on skeletal remains in New South Wales, in Bosnia, in Kosovo, and in East Timor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I can turn now, Dr. Lawrence, just to your visit previously to this Tribunal in the Krstic trial, and the work that you did in Bosnia. Could you tell us very briefly about your position in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I was the chief forensic pathologist for the ICTY in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in that role what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: My duties were to coordinate the mortuary portion of the investigation, exhumation, and autopsy process; to supervise and to perform autopsies on the remains; to supervise the activities of the anthropologists, the pathologists, and the other staff members at the mortuary; and to formulate a report summarising the results of the -- the autopsy procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are the reports that you prepared following that work the reports that you testified about in Krstic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you done any further work on these matters since the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, as you know, because your reports are already tendered in evidence, then I'm not going to ask you any further about the contents of those -- those documents. I just, as a last question, I would like to ask about the materials that you brought with you here today. Could you tell me briefly what those are, please?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes. They consist of the eight reports from the individual sites. They also include -- at the front of each of those reports is a summary document. I have a -- a list of the summary documents, and I also, at the time of the Krstic trial, prepared a summary document stating the overall numbers based on the summary documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Lawrence. And please, for any future answer, if you wish to refer to those documents, please do so, just please let us know.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Elderkin. Now, who is going first from the Defence teams? Mr. Lazarevic, you had indicated about one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And I think I will stick to this estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. We'll have a break in about 30 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I notice that, Mr. Haynes, your client hasn't been wearing the headphones or earphones throughout the entire sitting. Is there a problem with them, or is it because he can follow the proceedings just the same? You can consult with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if there is something that we ought to address, we ought to know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has a difficulty with the headphones directly on to his ears. I believe this is known to the court staff. It wasn't to me previously, but he is able to hear them sufficiently with the headphones draped around his neck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But if that creates any insurmountable problems, then please tell us and we will find a remedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very kind of you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic. I'm so sorry for having interrupted you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- before you had even started. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, we received from the OTP your curriculum vitae, and Mr. Elderkin covered some of that with you. You worked as the main forensic pathologist from May to October, 1998 in Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how that came about for you to become involved in the work of the OTP of the ICTY in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I was going to provide some assistance to the ICTY in 1997. Due to unforeseen circumstances, there was no need for my work in 1997. In early 1998, I was contacted by the ICTY, who were looking for a forensic pathologist to work for them for six months. I was approached with a number of other pathologists. We did a phone interview, and I was offered the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So it was your initiative that led to your involvement?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes, to some degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After becoming appointed as pathologist in the Prosecutor's office of the ICTY, I assume that you received some briefings, that the Prosecutor's office provided some instructions to you as to your duties, as well as to what you might expect in Bosnia and what is expected of you there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who provided that initial briefing to you as to what had happened in Srebrenica in 1995 in the opinion of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: That's difficult to remember. I got information from many people, and I honestly cannot remember who told me what, but I had spoken to Graham Blewitt, John Ralston, members of the investigation team, Professor Richard Wright. So I -- I received information from a large number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Naturally, you cannot be expected to remember every word that was uttered to you, and by whom. But could you summarise the information that was provided to you in OTP -- by OTP as to what was their impression about what had happened in Srebrenica in July of 1995? What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I -- I was told that a number of people had been killed, that they had been buried, that the graves had been then re -- dug up, and that the bodies had been reburied again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. So you were expected to prove, or rather, to find evidence that what you just described to us happened indeed in that way?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: No. My job, as a forensic pathologist in this, along with everything else I do, is to test the information that I have been given to see if it is true. In the course of any investigation that I do, I am given information, but it is my job to test that information to see if it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When preparing to go out to work in the field, were you perhaps told that in the territory of Srebrenica municipality, as well as in neighbouring municipalities of Bratunac and Zvornik, in 1992 very intense combat took place between the Serbian and Muslim forces, which is to say that this happened some three years before the 1995 event -- sorry, 1995 events.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I was aware there had been previous combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Was your attention drawn to the fact that in doing your work, you should bear in mind that some of the graves that you might come across were created in 1992 or 1993? Were you told to pay particular attention to that fact?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you were never told by the Prosecution before going to Bosnia that there existed certain mass graves in the territory of Zvornik and Bratunac dating back to 1992. Did they have such information?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: No. I don't recall being given -- told that specifically. I was aware that there were graves there, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When digging up those graves, you never tried to establish the time of death; namely, whether the people buried there died in 1992, 1993, or 1995? At least, I was unable to find this information in any of the reports provided to us by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I should point out that I wasn't doing the digging, that that was carried on by Richard Wright and questions in regard to that should probably be directed to him. But, yes, it is extremely difficult to ascertain the time of death based on the normal techniques that a forensic pathologist would use in those graves. I do understand, however, that there were some items that were recovered by other people in the graves, which suggested that at least in some of the graves there was evidence that these -- these must have come from -- a time later than -- sorry, 1992, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Perhaps this question should have been addressed to Mr. Wright. But from your point of view, as a forensic pathologist, would that affect the autopsy report that you drafted, the fact that the body you are analysing is the body of a person who died a couple of years before 1995?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: From the examination of the bodies alone, I could not ascertain the time of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before you went to Bosnia, as you were receiving the briefing in the Prosecution, were you told that a large column of Srebrenica Muslims, many of whom were armed, attempted to break through in the territory under the control of the army of Republika Srpska, leading to Tuzla, and that this column suffered great losses in the course of that attempted break-through?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I studied the reports that you drafted concerning the autopsies of bodies found in mass graves or in graves, and I'd like now to turn to a fact that figures in many of those reports; for example, report on remains at Liplje 2, you said that no weapons were found on any bodies, no bodies were dressed in either military or police uniform. When speaking of Zeleni Jadar 5, you said that no body had a weapon it and that no body was in a police or military uniform. The same statement can be found on your report on Cancari Road, 3.4, as well as in all our other reports, except for the one about Kozluk. Thus, can you tell me whether you received from the Prosecution any instructions about you paying attention to any weapons or uniforms, or did you consider yourself this fact to be of such importance that it required that you mentioned it in your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I was not given instructions on how to write the reports. I did tend to follow pattern of the reports done by pathologists from the previous year. I was aware that one of the possible explanations for the deaths was that they were in fact deaths in combat. And therefore, I did consider it relevant to include the fact, as to whether or not I found people in uniform and people who had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood your answer correctly, you believe that finding weapons in mass graves and finding bodies dressed in uniforms is important in order to establish whether the deceased was a civilian or a military serviceman?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: It's one of the points of evidence which might answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is why it is included in your report, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: See here, before this Court, we have heard a number of testimonies of survivors from Srebrenica, who said that they were members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but that they were never issued with uniforms. Some of them said that they didn't even have any weapons. What I just told you, this fact, were you ever told this by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to put a couple of general questions to you concerning what is termed as primary and secondary graves in the reports. Can you explain to us on what basis do you draw a distinction between a primary and a secondary grave?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I would not claim to be able to tell the difference between a primary and secondary grave; that would have been information provided to me by Richard Wright, who is the expert on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: However, since these terms are mentioned very frequently in these documents, can you tell us what was your criterium when using these terms, primary and secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I -- as I say, I would rely on Richard Wright to make that assessment. I am -- I did attend two of the grave sites, but I would not claim expertise in being able to tell you which is a primary and which is a secondary site.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [In English] Excuse me for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your research, I suppose that you established also the number of bodies found in graves?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Again, and I don't want to be -- to sound to be evasive, that was largely the job of the forensic anthropologist, Mr. Jose-Pablo Baraybar. I did include those numbers in my report because I think it was impossible to understand my report without that information. But the calculations in that have been performed by Mr. Baraybar, and questions on that should be directed to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for telling me this. So if I understood you well, your report does contain such information, but the source of that information is not you, but rather Mr. Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, would you please assist us with establishing more specific time references as to when the exhumations were done at these local sites, exhumations on which you worked. I will cover this briefly and if I make any mistakes, would you please correct me. So if I understood you well, the first of these autopsies conducted by was in relation to the dam, and it was in July of 1998. That was the first site where you worked, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Following that, based on the data that I have, in August of 1998 you worked on the Cancari Road, site number 12?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And then thereafter in August and September of 1998, you worked on site number 3 on Cancari Road?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to assist us with this: We have your report on the bodies found near Kozluk in 1998. But since we never found any time reference as to when this was done, could you assist us with that to your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I would need to refer to my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are entitled to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. My involvement in the site at Kozluk was essentially one day. The data on that is included at the back of Cancari Road 3. It does not include the date at which that examination was performed. It was just one day, and it would have been after the completion of CR 3 and probably during the examinations of the Hadzici Road cases, but I cannot give you the specific date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This does give us a closer time reference. Following that, I can see that all other sites where you worked were the sites covering in October of 1998; Hadzici 3, Zeleni Jadar 5, and Liplje 2. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And can you just tell me chronologically which one came first and which one was the next one?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I -- as I recall, there were several. Hadzici road 3, 4, and 5 were done in parallel. At that stage, we had a larger number of teams working up to nine teams; and from recollection, I think some of the different sites were done at different times. My recall, it was probably Hadzici 3 then 5 then 4, but I'm not completely certain about that. I could refer to my notes, if it was -- if it was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's not of major importance, but I wanted to see something else. Zeleni Jadar and Liplje, did you work there before or after Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: After.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [In English] Your Honour, is it time for our usual break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. We will have a 25-minute break, and then we will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, I wanted to move to a different topic now, compared to what we covered up to now. It generally relates to the problems that you encountered during your autopsy work. What I would like to do is cite a couple of things for you and see if you agree with that. The first one is that, "In a normal situation a decision on whether an injury was sustained while the person was alive or if it's a post-mortem one is to a large agree based on the observation of surrounding tissue and things that can be connected with that, such as bruises, swellings, and bleeding. "In a decomposed body in which tissue changes colour very quickly and starts to break off, this becomes very difficult; and if the post-mortem remains are already skeletonised, then it's impossible. Before healing begins it will look just the same as a fracture weeks before or after death. The existence of bruises is the only thing that can differentiate between such injuries." Do you agree with such an assessment?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a general statement. I would like to make another general statement. "While we have incompletely decomposed bodies, it's practically to be sure if any of the cited injuries were sustained while the person was alive, and theoretically all the injuries could have been post-mortem ones, even those which were quite evidently injuries from -- or wounds from fire-arms." Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: In rare cases there was still evidence of haemorrhage, but these would be a very small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a general example what I read to you is accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All the reports that you drafted were drafted on the assumption that a large majority of fire-arms wounds and other relevant wounds found on the bodies were inflicted during -- while the persons were still alive and were the cause of death. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes, that was my general assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Even without such an assumption, that the wounds were inflicted when the persons were still alive and they were the cause of death, any further analysis would be irrelevant or pointless, wouldn't it? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes, it's very difficult to make any further assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The reports that were presented to us, your reports on the basis of them, I see that you did not attempt to establish the locations where the persons whose autopsies you performed and that were found in the graves actually lost their lives. All you focused on was the cause of death. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I -- I completely understand what you're getting at there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, of course, I could put it in a different way. You did not thus investigate or were able to learn when, how, and under which circumstances the persons lost their lives. I am thinking of course of the bodies that you performed autopsies on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer, because that makes it more compounded, for sure. I think you better go back to your previous question, and I'll intervene here and then take over after me, Mr. Lazarevic. Your previous question was the following: "The reports that were presented to us, your reports on the bases of them, I see that you did not attempt to establish the locations where the persons whose autopsies you performed that were found in the graves actually lost their live. All you focused was the cause of death, is that correct?" So I will rephrase the question first. In your role as a forensic pathologist, did you at any time while performing these autopsies attempt to establish the location where these -- those persons came from, or were located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time that they were killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or at the time they were buried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were some injuries, for example, gun-shot wounds going through the heart; gun-shot wounds in the brain; in a small number of them there was clear evidence of haemorrhage, these would be rapidly fatal. So it would be safe to assume that they died where they were shot, but this is the vast minority of the cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you did not try to -- did not attempt to establish the location, did you? And if not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if not, why didn't you? This is basically the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think because the problems that have been alluded to in ascertaining at what time the injuries occurred, as I say, in some of the injuries which were clearly rapidly fatal, I think there is little doubt that they occurred at the place at which they were shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And the second question that Mr. Lazarevic put to you, which I described as compound, has one particular or more than one particular issue that you need to address. In your work did you try to establish how and under which circumstances the persons lost their lives? Was that part of your work or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I think you can take it up from there. I tried to cover both questions, singling out the various matters. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] By all means, Your Honour, and I'm grateful for you to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Going through your reports, I found different data about how the bodies that you examined had gun-shot wounds and wounds from the front, inflicted from the back and inflicted from the side and those inflicted from above. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Based on this fact, can we conclude that the position of the persons, which were shot at the time, as well as the position of persons who shot at them were very different, that in that sense there is no common denominator for all the bodies that were examined?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: If you look at the figures in which we could tell whether they were shot from -- in front or behind, in majority of the cases I could not tell. It is therefore very difficult to make any prediction. Since most of the cases one couldn't tell with certainty, I don't think we had enough reliable data to ascertain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely the answer to my question. We cannot have one common conclusion for all the bodies in terms of their position, how they were shot, from which position, from what distance, what weapon was used. There can be no uniform conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes, there is too much -- there are too many variables there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Other than the gun-shot wounds, a certain number of bodies featured traces of shrapnel, shrapnel wounds, as well as wounds that were not either gun-shot wounds or wounds from an explosive device and so on, and this also is contained in your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now like to move to another topic. In your reports, I noticed on a couple of occasions that the term "ligatures" was used. Can you please tell us what you specifically understand that term to mean, the term "ligature" or "ligatures"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: In forensic pathology, the term "ligature" is usually applied to a band which is applied around part of the body; for example, wrist bindings, ankle bindings, or in some cases around the neck in the cases of strangulation or hanging.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course, a ligature can also be a piece of fabric that was torn or ripped to the necessary width and length to use it for the required purpose. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have heard the testimony before this Tribunal of a witness who worked at the Srebrenica hospital in 1995. This witness said that at that time in Srebrenica, there was a lack of medical equipment and supplies,; and in July 1995, all kinds of things were used to dress wounds. Other than bandages, strips of cloth were also used. I assume that you don't know about this, do you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
