utterances.text: No. There were some bodies that did actually have bandages on them. However, the -- and, in fact, in one particular case one did have a bandage and a wrist binding as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you one more thing on this subject. Did the Prosecution ever draw your attention to the fact that throughout the war in Bosnia different units belonging both to the Serb Muslim and the Croat side very frequently wore bands around their arms as recognition signs during their actions? Were you ever told this?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you rule out the possibility that these improvised bandages and these bands that were worn were actually what you found in the autopsies in the mass graves?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On what basis?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: On some of the bodies, the ligatures were clearly wrapped around both of the wrist -- of the wrists, and they were still held in position. In some of the cases, the arms were clearly secured behind the body. I have little doubt, in fact, no doubt that they were wrist bindings and not some form of insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But in some locations such strips of fabrics were found that were not specifically connected to any body; they were found outside of that. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes. I agree that there were some -- and I have included in my report those that I thought were definitely wrist bindings and that's that could have been. The point I need to make is that there were tremendous similarities between the ones which were secure on the wrists and the ones that were found in the grave, which would lead me to conclude that they probably were ligatures. But I agree, in the absence of clear evidence that they were around the wrists, you could not be certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. In your reports, you treated separately whole bodies and body parts that were found in the graves that were autopsied, and the body parts that were found were treated in your reports as an actual person. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to put to you a hypothetical question; and since you are an expert, I believe that you will be able to answer it. If an arm belonging to a person was found in a secondary grave and in a completely different secondary grave the other arm was found belonging to the same person, in your reports, this would appear to be two persons or two bodies that were found. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Not exactly. I have given you figures on causes of death for the complete bodies and then for the incomplete bodies. I think the information on the complete bodies is fairly reliable, but it's obviously extremely difficult in an incomplete body to conclude whether or not there were one person killed or two people killed. It just wasn't possible. I -- if we had been able to match every one of the bodies, it may have been possible. The reason I have included both information on the whole bodies and the body parts is, I think, in particularly some of the more disrupted graves such as Liplje, it -- it would be hard to get any useful information. I also needed to indicate, I think, how many gun-shot wounds we had. But I agree, it -- it is very difficult unless you can completely reunite all of the body parts to interpret exactly what the results on the body parts means in terms of an actual cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to have the complete picture practically, you would need to do a DNA analysis of each body part found in order to establish whether it belonged to the same person; for example, a tooth, a part of a skull, a part of a hand?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes. And given the mixtures of bodies, I think we had up to -- sometimes up to 14 individuals in a body bag, I think the process would be extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand your answer correctly, according to your best recollection, that kind of comparison and that kind of analysis was actually never carried out?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: We were always attempting to match bodies, and in some cases it would be because of clothing or because of an abnormality, we were able to do so, but that's a very small number. And at that stage we did not have the amount of DNA evidence available, which would have allowed you to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have a couple of questions left. When I looked at an object from a sketch that I found, this is Prosecution Exhibit P638, I noticed that the conclusion of the entire forensic team was that the mass grave in Zeleni Jadar actually constituted a secondary grave compared to Glogova 2. Is that the conclusion that you drew as a team?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I'm -- I wasn't the person primarily tasked with doing that. Again, that would come down to Richard Wright. But I certainly believe that the remains that we saw in Zeleni Jadar probably relate to the warehouse at Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question on that subject. According to your findings relating to locality 5 in Zeleni Jadar, according to the assessments or the estimates that a grave contained at least 150 bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That number of at least 150 is relatively indefinite in the sense that you did not give us any range. When you said at least 150, can that also mean 160 or perhaps 200?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: As I think I've already pointed out to you, the minimum number of individuals was calculated by Mr. Baraybar, and that question should properly be put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm also going to do that. I'm going to take your advice. I have just one more question strictly relating to your area of expertise. On the basis of changes on a body, can it be definitely established whether a body was exhumed from a primary or a secondary grave? Only on the basis of changes on the actual body?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I think that depends on what's present. If you find some injuries in particular sites, you might suspect that it indicates a secondary grave, but it depends on the period between burial and recovery. It in general was possible to pick some of the injuries that had occurred during the last exhumation, but it was difficult to pick the differences between the primary and secondary sites just purely without knowing the further information. Again, I would routinely not be performing that examination, that would be rightfully what Richard Wright's job would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Doctor. I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lazarevic. Who is going next? Madam Fauveau. You had indicated 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But I think I need less than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you drafted many reports on the autopsies you performed on the exhumed bodies in various sites that were allegedly connected with the events in Srebrenica. Is it fair to say that in each report part of the reports was devoted to the procedure, the method utilised for the autopsy, and prior to the autopsy?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In each of your reports, you stated that the clothes had been removed and then washed. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As to the bodies themselves, they were washed before they were autopsied?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: They were photographed, undressed, examined, and then washed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Before the clothing was washed, before the bodies were washed, the traces or residues, be it soil or vegetation, was it collected on the bodies and on the clothes?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: No. My understanding is that the soil samples were taken at the site. The problem being that by the time they had been transported and -- there could have been contamination, so those soil samples, as a general rule, should have been taken at the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You say that there could have been contaminated during transport. Does this mean that indeed the transportation from the exhumation site to the mortuary was not done according to the rules?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: No. I -- I believe it was done as well as it could be done, but these were bodies that were quite badly decomposed. They were bodies that were quite badly broken up. From my experience of examining bodies in the grave and then in the mortuary, there was some movement of material. It was inevitable, I think, given the state of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that traces of vegetation, grass, or other substances that could be found on bodies or clothing can indeed identify the place, the location where the people were killed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe in Zeleni Jadar there was in fact some hay, which I believe was also identified at Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree to say that if somebody had been detained before they were killed, similar traces can show where the person was detained?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Who's next? Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Lawrence, just a few questions to follow up on the questions put by my colleague. It remained unclear to me what method you used and how you established the minimum number of persons at one site, which is a category featuring in all of your reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Again, I need to reiterate that it was not my responsibility to ascertain the minimum number of individuals. That was performed by the chief anthropologist. I have included the data because it makes meaningful the other data. It wasn't intended to state that it was my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In your report, you specifically dealt at dam and Liplje 2 sites, you dealt with primary and secondary graves. Did you compare the minimum number, or rather the body parts in these two sites, and did you try to arrive at a composite number, to reconcile the numbers?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I -- I am not qualified to answer that question. You need to ask Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Nikolic. I have on the list remaining the Popovic team, the Pandurevic team, and the Beara team. The Beara team asking for 45 minutes. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I would like to clarify some of the answers you gave to my colleague, Mr. Lazarevic. It has to do with the burial, or rather with the weapons that would in a way imply that the victims in a grave were victims of an armed conflict. Could you please clarify whether in the course of your work you had similar situations where a victim of an armed conflict, or to be more precise, a participant to an armed conflict, is buried with his or her weapon?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that you answered a question of Mr. Lazarevic saying that before you went to the location, before you started working on this, you received certain instructions from the Prosecution, or rather from the investigators, could you tell us whether anybody informed you that there is such a custom in Bosnia and Herzegovina that a victim of an armed conflict is buried with a weapon?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I was a bit imprecise. I said a victim of an armed conflict, and I wanted to say a participant of an armed conflict. I'm referring to a soldier who was killed.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: The answer is still no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you then tell me why did you consider this to be a potential indicator as to whether this was a participant in an armed conflict or a victim whose cause of death could have been somewhat different?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Because I thought it would -- it was one criteria that might specify between them. I didn't say it was necessarily a good criteria, but it is a criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that this criterium was selected by you in this particular case, or is this a criterium that you used previously in your other work?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I think, from memory, the criterium was used by my predecessor, and I think that's why I included the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell me who was your predecessor?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Bill -- Dr. Bill Hunt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the accurate spelling of the name, as it reads in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he also perform autopsies in Bosnia? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes, he was the chief pathologist in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, he was the one who introduced the method. He was the one who introduced the criterium which was then used in research, analysis, identification of a victim?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to put another question to you, which has to do with ligatures. You already discussed this with Mr. Lazarevic, but I need another clarification. You said that in certain graves there were pieces of fabric which resembled ligatures, but were not tied around ankles or body parts of victims.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Did you attempt to obtain information as to whether such as fabric was used for some other purpose, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what -- what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to explain. You will have heard that a number of Muslim soldiers, members of Muslim forces, did not have uniforms, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm not sure whether you were also informed that in order to have some sort of a distinction, they wore some arm bands on their clothing, since they did not have any uniform. Did you hear of this fact?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question has been asked and answered already, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all. I will not have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That leaves us with Mr. Haynes and Mr. Ostojic. I'm asking Mr. Haynes, first, because if you really need 45 minutes, I would rather suggest that you take one whole stretch rather than have it in parts. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't presently have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So let's start with you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, are you here for any particular purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was getting a little bored upstairs. No. I have the next witness, and I always have the fear that I'm suddenly going to be watching the monitor and hearing no questions, no questions, they've answered by my colleagues. That's why I rushed down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope that doesn't amount to anxiety neurosis, but anyway let's start with Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. To put you at ease, I don't have 45 minutes and I hope to conclude in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop in seven minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, earlier this afternoon, when you were asked by my learned friend Mr. Lazarevic, on page 78 and 79, he asked you just so we can put in context, "Do you believe that finding weapons in mass grave and finding bodies dressed in uniforms is important in order to establish whether the deceased was a civilian or a military serviceman." And you answer, which appears on line 4 of page 79, is, "It's one of points of evidence which might answer that question." Do you remember that generally?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What other points might help us answer that question?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I -- I think the circumstances -- I find it difficult to believe that people who are blindfolded and have their hands tied behind their backs are probably combatants at the time that they are in fact killed. I guess the other things are the general patterns of injuries that you expect to see. In modern combat, one would normally expect to see a lot of the casualties come from shrapnel, explosive devices. It verifies from conflict to conflict, but you would expect the majority of people to have shrapnel injuries in a conflict, not gun-shot wounds, so the high -- the high number of gun-shot wounds would be odd in those circumstances. The other thing that, frankly, I found odd was that, and this applies in forensic pathology generally, when you found that somebody has gone to some effort to conceal the body, particularly to bury them and rebury them, it's usually an indication that they're trying conceal a death. And I don't understand why someone would go to so much trouble if these were just armed conflict deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any other reasons that might help us answer that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: No. I think those are the ones that come to mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your report, sir, I noticed you had a section captioned "range of fire." Can you tell me what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes. In dealing with gun-shot wounds, traditionally, the forensic pathologist is supposed to make some form of assessment as to whether the gun was held in contact with the body, within a metre of the body, or at a greater distance than that. And the way you tell is by the presence of gunpowder residue around the wound. In this case, I think I saw one case which might have indicated some gunpowder residue; but I think given the state of decomposition, it would have been almost impossible to ascertain the range of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In parts of your report, you also identify, I think, or define decomposition by another term, which I think it's --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Disarticulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Disarticulation, that's it. Are those synonymous words?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: No. A body can be skeletonised but still in continuity so that the arms are attached, the neck is attached, the head is attached. Disarticulation refers to the separation of the limbs. So in a fully fleshed body, you could, for example, see separation of the upper part of the torso and the lower part of the torso, as the body was rolled through the grave. Now, that would be disarticulated but still relatively reserved. The two are slightly different concepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the context of range of fire, was it impossible to determine what the range of fire was because of the decomposition and the skeletonisation of the body?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was extremely hard to. I -- I guess it's possible to do testing on the clothing; but given the degree of contamination, I suspect that it probably would have been difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your reports, you actually when you mention range of fire, and I think you don't in all of them, but I'll defer to you on that. On most, when you mention range of fire, you say that the assessment is not only difficult but impossible?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes, I think largely it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to -- and again I'm not familiar with the process of washing the corpse, but what happens to the bullet fragments or the shrapnel that remains near or around the body?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: In some cases, if it was easily retrievable, that would have occurred during the process of fluoroscopy so that you could locate exactly where it was. In some cases, you would wash the external portion to see if you could find the bullet holes and then perform a dissection. Sometimes it became necessary to go back to fluoroscopy to recover the bullet fragment if it couldn't be recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We talked -- you mentioned a little bit about disarticulation. I want to understand it. When a corpse is decomposed or skeletonised, does it render the fact or does it reasonably conclude that parts of that skeleton will dissociate itself with other parts of the body, if you will?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes. Once it gets do complete skeletonisation, you will get fairly rapid disarticulation, but there are some cases where ligaments decompose slower so you get basic retention of the position of the body. In the skeletonised bodies that I normally deal with that have been buried, they will be decomposed but not disarticulated because the bodies have been disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in the autopsies that you performed, I think 888, is it, approximately?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Those were the -- that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Under your direction?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes. That's the total number of individuals I think were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What per cent were skeletonised?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: That varied from site to site. At the dam, almost all of them; at Hadzici road, I think almost 80, 90 per cent were fully fleshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever do analysis for all the sites that you have actually done autopsies for?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: I have figures for them. Liplje and the dam were the most decomposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does that mean skeletonised? Not to interrupt you, because you did make a distinction? I just wanted you to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE.
utterances.text: Yes. They were both disarticulated and decomposed. And Hadzici road 5 was the best, both in terms of articulation, but also in terms of lack of decomposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we have to stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then Your Honour, just so -- if I could may. I won't have the doctor come back unless someone else has questions. I'm pretty much done, Your Honour. Just if that's okay. Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any re-examination in which case it will be left for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, we're finished with your testimony, and I wish to thank Mr. Ostojic for his pragmatic approach. We thank you for having come over to give testimony and we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
